modernLocation.en: Patmos island, Dodecanese, Greece

summary.en: Small Aegean island where, by his own account, John was exiled 'for the word of God' and received the visions of Revelation (Revelation 1:9). The traditional Cave of the Apocalypse is a major pilgrimage site.

modernLocation.en: Pamukkale, Denizli Province, Turkey

summary.en: Phrygian city near Laodicea and Colossae where strong tradition (and an excavated martyrium) places the ministry and death of the apostle Philip.

modernLocation.en: Alexandria, Egypt

summary.en: Great Hellenistic city of Egypt; church tradition credits Mark the Evangelist with founding its Christian community and serving as its first bishop.

modernLocation.en: Tell el-Muqayyar, Dhi Qar Governorate, southern Iraq

summary.en: A major Sumerian city (excavated by Woolley, with its great ziggurat of Ur-Nammu) named as Abraham's birthplace in Genesis 11:31. A minority of scholars instead locate the biblical 'Ur of the Chaldeans' in the north near Haran; the southern Tell el-Muqayyar remains the traditional identification.

modernLocation.en: Harran, Şanlıurfa Province, southeastern Turkey

summary.en: An ancient caravan city on the Balikh where, in Genesis, Terah's family settled and Abraham was later called on toward Canaan (Genesis 12:4). Long a cult center of the moon-god Sin.

modernLocation.en: Tell Balata, at the eastern edge of modern Nablus, West Bank

summary.en: Abraham's first altar site in Canaan (Genesis 12:6-7) and a recurring covenant place through Jacob and Joshua. The excavated Middle-Bronze city at Tell Balata includes a massive fortress-temple.

modernLocation.en: Beitin, West Bank, ~17 km north of Jerusalem (traditional identification)

summary.en: Where Abraham built an altar and Jacob dreamed of the ladder to heaven and named the place 'house of God' (Genesis 28). The identification with Beitin is traditional and debated (some prefer el-Bireh).

modernLocation.en: Old city of Hebron, West Bank

summary.en: Abraham bought the cave of Machpelah as a burial place for Sarah (Genesis 23); tradition holds Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and their wives are entombed there, beneath the Herodian-era enclosure still standing today.

modernLocation.en: Tel Be'er Sheva, Negev, southern Israel (UNESCO World Heritage 'Biblical Tel')

summary.en: The southern frontier of the patriarchs, associated with Abraham's and Isaac's wells and covenants (Genesis 21, 26); 'from Dan to Beersheba' marked Israel's extent. The Iron-Age town at Tel Be'er Sheva has a famous horned altar.

modernLocation.en: Qantir, eastern Nile Delta, Egypt

summary.en: The eastern-Delta region where Genesis settles Jacob's family and where Exodus 1:11 has the Israelites building the store-city of Raamses. The Ramesside capital Pi-Rameses is firmly located at Qantir, above the earlier Hyksos capital Avaris.

modernLocation.en: Jebel Musa, southern Sinai Peninsula, Egypt (traditional; other candidates proposed)

disputes.en: The mountain of the Law has no secure identification. The Byzantine tradition (St Catherine's Monastery) fixes it at Jebel Musa in the southern Sinai, but scholars have proposed Jebel Serbal, Har Karkom in the Negev, and sites in NW Arabia (e.g. Jebel al-Lawz); none is archaeologically confirmed.

summary.en: The mountain where, in Exodus, Moses received the Law and Israel entered the covenant. Its location is genuinely uncertain; the traditional Jebel Musa is used here with alternatives noted.

modernLocation.en: Tell el-Qudeirat, northeastern Sinai, near the Israel-Egypt border

summary.en: The wilderness base from which Israel sent spies into Canaan and where they lingered many years (Numbers 13; 20). Widely, though not universally, identified with the spring at Tell el-Qudeirat.

modernLocation.en: Mount Nebo, Madaba Governorate, Jordan

summary.en: The ridge east of the Jordan from which Moses viewed the promised land and where he died (Deuteronomy 34); a Byzantine memorial church with famous mosaics crowns the summit today.

modernLocation.en: Egypt; Coptic tradition venerates sites along the Nile (Old Cairo / Abu Serga, Wadi El Natrun, Asyut)

disputes.en: The Egyptian refuge is nowhere located in the text; the mapped point marks Old Cairo (Abu Serga), one of several sites Coptic tradition associates with the Holy Family's stay, not an archaeologically fixed location.

summary.en: Egypt was the Holy Family's refuge after Joseph, warned in a dream, fled Herod's massacre of the infants of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:13-15), staying until Herod's death — 'Out of Egypt I called my son' (Hosea 11:1). The exact place is unknown; the mapped point marks Old Cairo (Abu Serga), one of several Coptic-tradition refuge sites. LEG: land arrival and return.

modernLocation.en: Tell Fara, Al-Qādisiyyah Governorate, southern Iraq

summary.en: Sumerian city on the Euphrates flood plain, home of Ziusudra — the flood hero of the oldest Mesopotamian deluge tradition, paralleled by Utnapishtim in Gilgamesh and by the Genesis narrative. Excavations found a river-flood silt layer here (c. 2900 BC). Scripture does not name where Noah built the ark; this site anchors the Mesopotamian setting of the tradition.

modernLocation.en: Mount Ararat massif, Iğdır/Ağrı Provinces, Türkiye — with candidate sites at Durupınar and Mount Cudi

disputes.en: Genesis 8:4 names a region — 'the mountains of Ararat' (Urartu) — not a peak. Later tradition fixed on Greater Mount Ararat (5,137 m, mapped here); the boat-shaped Durupınar formation 30 km south is urged by recent survey teams; older Syriac and Islamic tradition points to Mount Cudi far to the southwest. No candidate is archaeologically confirmed.

label.en: Durupınar formation, near Üzengili (GPS 39.4406° N, 44.2347° E) — GPR scans 2019, soil analyses 2022–2024
Mount Cudi (Cudi Dağı) — Syriac, Quranic and early tradition

summary.en: Where 'the ark rested … upon the mountains of Ararat' (Genesis 8:4). Ararat is biblical Urartu, the mountain country around Lake Van. Tradition since the Middle Ages favors Greater Mount Ararat; the Durupınar formation nearby has drawn recent ground-penetrating-radar and soil studies whose ark claims geologists dispute as a natural syncline; Mount Cudi carries the oldest extra-biblical landing tradition.

modernLocation.en: Near Hillah, Babil Governorate, Iraq (site of Babylon)

summary.en: The plain in southern Mesopotamia where, after the Flood, the nations descended from Noah's sons settled and built the tower of Babel (Genesis 11:2-4). Mapped at Babylon, the city Genesis links to the name Babel.

modernLocation.en: Nein, Lower Galilee, Israel — on the northwest slope of the Hill of Moreh, ~12 km south-southeast of Nazareth

summary.en: The Galilean village where Luke records Jesus raising a widow's only son as the funeral procession left the gate (Luke 7:11-17) — the first raising of the dead in the Gospels. The Arab village of Nein preserves the ancient name, and the identification has been continuous since the Byzantine period; a Franciscan chapel marks the traditional spot.

modernLocation.en: Lod, Israel, on the coastal plain ~18 km southeast of Tel Aviv

summary.en: A town of the Sharon plain (Old Testament Lod, 1 Chronicles 8:12) where Peter, itinerating among the coastal congregations, healed the paralysed Aeneas — 'and all the residents of Lydda and Sharon saw him, and they turned to the Lord' (Acts 9:32-35). Modern Lod continuously preserves the name and site.

modernLocation.en: Jaffa (Yafo), the old-city port on the south side of Tel Aviv, Israel; the traditional House of Simon the Tanner stands in the old city

summary.en: The ancient Mediterranean port of Judea (Jonah's embarkation point, Jonah 1:3). In Acts, Peter raised the disciple Tabitha (Dorcas) from death here (Acts 9:36-43), stayed with Simon the tanner, and on the housetop received the vision of the sheet that opened the gospel to the Gentiles (Acts 10). The old city of Jaffa preserves the site.

ancientName.en: Valley of Siddim (the Salt Sea basin)

modernLocation.en: Southern basin of the Dead Sea (traditional); exact field unknown

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: The 'vale of Siddim, which is the salt sea' (Genesis 14:3), full of bitumen pits, where the four Mesopotamian kings under Chedorlaomer defeated the five cities of the plain and carried off Lot — prompting Abram's night pursuit and rescue. The traditional location is the shallow southern basin of the Dead Sea; no site has been identified.

modernLocation.en: Tell Hisban, Jordan, ~20 km southwest of Amman

summary.en: Capital of Sihon king of the Amorites, taken by Israel on the march up the King's Highway when Sihon refused passage and gave battle at Jahaz (Numbers 21:21-31). Tell Hisban preserves the name; its excavated Iron Age remains post-date the conquest debate, one strand of the wider dating question.

modernLocation.en: Daraa, southern Syria, on the Yarmouk tributaries

summary.en: Where 'Og the king of Bashan went out against them... to battle at Edrei' (Numbers 21:33) and was defeated, giving Israel the Bashan plateau. The name survives continuously in modern Daraa.

modernLocation.en: Tell es-Sultan, beside modern Jericho, West Bank — the world's oldest walled town

summary.en: The fortified oasis city whose walls fell to Joshua after seven days of circuits (Joshua 6) — the opening act of the conquest. Tell es-Sultan shows collapsed mudbrick ramparts and a burn layer; whether that destruction dates to c. 1400 BC (Garstang, Wood) or c. 1550 BC (Kenyon) is the classic conquest-archaeology debate.

modernLocation.en: et-Tell near Deir Dibwan, West Bank (majority identification; Khirbet el-Maqatir is the main rival)

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: The second city of the conquest: Israel's initial repulse (Achan's sin), then its capture by ambush (Joshua 7-8). The majority site, et-Tell, was unoccupied in the Late Bronze Age — the sharpest identification problem in conquest archaeology; Khirbet el-Maqatir has been proposed as an alternative.

modernLocation.en: el-Jib, West Bank, ~9 km northwest of Jerusalem

summary.en: The Hivite city that made peace with Joshua by ruse and was then defended by him against the five Amorite kings — the day of hailstones and the sun standing still (Joshua 10). Jar handles stamped 'gb'n' from el-Jib's great rock-cut pool confirmed the identification; the pool itself figures in 2 Samuel 2:13.

ancientName.en: Hazor, 'the head of all those kingdoms'

modernLocation.en: Tel Hazor, Upper Galilee, Israel, ~14 km north of the Sea of Galilee

summary.en: The largest Canaanite city of the land (~80 ha), seat of Jabin, head of the northern coalition crushed at the waters of Merom — 'and he burnt Hazor with fire' (Joshua 11:11-13). The tell's Late Bronze destruction layer, with burned palace and mutilated cult statues, is central to the conquest debate; the city rose again under Solomon (1 Kings 9:15) and fell to Tiglath-pileser III in 732 BC (2 Kings 15:29).

modernLocation.en: Mount Tabor, Lower Galilee, Israel, rising from the Jezreel valley

summary.en: The dome-shaped mountain where Barak mustered ten thousand of Naphtali and Zebulun at Deborah's word, descending on Sisera's nine hundred iron chariots as the Kishon swept them away (Judges 4-5).

modernLocation.en: Ma'ayan Harod at the foot of Mount Gilboa, Jezreel valley, Israel

summary.en: The spring where Gideon's army was sifted to three hundred by the manner of their drinking, before the night attack with torches and trumpets on the Midianite camp by the hill of Moreh (Judges 7).

modernLocation.en: Tell el-Ful, northern outskirts of Jerusalem (identification debated)

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: Benjamite town whose outrage against the Levite's concubine ignited Israel's first civil war — all the tribes against Benjamin, and Benjamin nearly annihilated (Judges 19-21). Later Saul's seat. Albright's identification with Tell el-Ful, though standard, remains debated.

modernLocation.en: Tell en-Nasbeh, ~12 km north of Jerusalem, West Bank

summary.en: Samuel's mustering point, where thunder routed the Philistines and the stone Ebenezer — 'hitherto hath the LORD helped us' — was raised (1 Samuel 7:5-14). Later fortified by Asa against Israel with the stones of dismantled Ramah (1 Kings 15:22).

modernLocation.en: Tel Afek, Rosh Ha'ayin, Israel, at the Yarkon springs

summary.en: The Philistine camp opposite Israel's at Ebenezer where the ark of the covenant was captured, Hophni and Phinehas killed, and Eli's line judged — 'the glory is departed from Israel' (1 Samuel 4). The same tell became Herod's Antipatris, where Paul spent a night under Roman escort (Acts 23:31).

modernLocation.en: Mukhmas, West Bank, above the Wadi Suweinit pass ~11 km northeast of Jerusalem

summary.en: Philistine forward camp between the crags Bozez and Seneh, where Jonathan and his armour-bearer scaled the pass and started the panic that Saul's muster turned into a rout (1 Samuel 13-14).

ancientName.en: Valley of Elah (between Socoh and Azekah)

modernLocation.en: The Elah valley, Israel, overlooked by Khirbet Qeiyafa; the brook of the five smooth stones runs its floor

summary.en: Where the armies faced off 'between Socoh and Azekah' and David met Goliath of Gath with a sling and a shepherd's staff (1 Samuel 17). The fortified early-10th-century site of Khirbet Qeiyafa above the valley bears directly on the debate over the kingdom David actually ruled.

modernLocation.en: Mount Gilboa ridge above the Jezreel valley, Israel

summary.en: Where Israel broke before the Philistines massed at Shunem: Saul's three sons fell, and the wounded king died on his own sword; the bodies were hung on the wall of Beth-shan (1 Samuel 31). David's lament: 'Ye mountains of Gilboa, let there be no dew' (2 Samuel 1:21).

modernLocation.en: The Citadel (Jabal al-Qal'a), Amman, Jordan

summary.en: Capital of Ammon, besieged by Joab while David remained in Jerusalem — the siege in which Uriah the Hittite was deliberately abandoned at the wall (2 Samuel 11); David later took 'the city of waters' and its crown (2 Samuel 12:26-31).

modernLocation.en: Tulul adh-Dhahab twin tells on the Jabbok (Zarqa) river, Jordan (leading candidate; identification uncertain)

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: Jacob's 'two camps' on the Jabbok, Ish-bosheth's Transjordan capital, and David's refuge during Absalom's revolt — the battle of the forest of Ephraim was fought nearby, 'and the wood devoured more people that day than the sword' (2 Samuel 18).

ancientName.en: Mount Zemaraim (in the hills of Ephraim)

modernLocation.en: Unidentified rise near the Bethel plateau, West Bank (Ras et-Tahuneh and others proposed)

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: Where Abijah of Judah, outnumbered two to one, addressed Jeroboam's Israel from the mountainside and then broke the double envelopment — Judah took Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron (2 Chronicles 13). The mountain itself has not been securely identified.

modernLocation.en: er-Ram, West Bank, ~8 km north of Jerusalem astride the north road

summary.en: The border town Baasha of Israel fortified 'that he might not suffer any to go out or come in to Asa king of Judah' — the chokepoint of the Israel-Judah border war, dismantled when Asa's silver turned Ben-hadad of Damascus against the north (1 Kings 15:16-22).

modernLocation.en: Tel Beit Shemesh, Israel, in the Sorek valley ~30 km west of Jerusalem

summary.en: Judahite border town where the ark returned from Philistia on a cart (1 Samuel 6) — and where, generations later, Jehoash of Israel captured Amaziah of Judah in the bluntest Israel-vs-Judah defeat, then broke down Jerusalem's wall and emptied the temple treasuries (2 Kings 14:11-14).

modernLocation.en: Sebastia, West Bank — the acropolis of Omri's hill

summary.en: Capital of the northern kingdom from Omri onward: Ahab's ivory house, Ben-hadad's failed siege (1 Kings 20), Elisha's famine siege lifted overnight (2 Kings 6-7), and at last the three-year Assyrian siege that ended the kingdom of Israel in 722 BC (2 Kings 17). Excavated palace quarter, ivories, and the Samaria ostraca survive.

ancientName.en: Aphek (east of the Sea of Galilee)

modernLocation.en: Golan Heights near modern 'Afiq, above En Gev (identification uncertain)

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: The Aphek of the Aramean wars, 'where a wall fell upon twenty and seven thousand of the men that were left' after Israel's victory over Ben-hadad (1 Kings 20:26-30), and where Elisha told Joash he would smite Aram (2 Kings 13:17). Distinct from the coastal Aphek; the eastern site is not securely identified.

modernLocation.en: Tell Qarqur, Orontes valley, northwest Syria

summary.en: Where Shalmaneser III's Assyrian army met a twelve-king coalition in 853 BC — including 'Ahab the Israelite' with 2,000 chariots and 10,000 soldiers, per the Kurkh Monolith. Unmentioned in Scripture, the battle is the linchpin synchronism that fixes the divided-kingdom chronology to absolute dates.

modernLocation.en: Tell er-Rumeith, northern Jordan (leading candidate; identification uncertain)

disputes.en: The identification of this site is debated; coordinates mark the leading candidate described in the summary.

summary.en: Levitical refuge city and perennial Israel-Aram flashpoint: Ahab fell here disguised in his chariot despite Micaiah's warning (1 Kings 22), and Joram's wounds from its later siege set the stage for Jehu's anointing in this same camp (2 Kings 8-9).

modernLocation.en: Tel Jezreel, Jezreel valley, Israel

summary.en: The Omride military enclosure and winter seat beside Naboth's vineyard — where Jehu's furious chariot drive ended with Joram dead in Naboth's field, Ahaziah of Judah mortally wounded, and Jezebel thrown from the window (2 Kings 9). The excavated Iron II casemate enclosure matches the dynasty's scale.

modernLocation.en: al-Karak, Jordan, beneath the Crusader castle

summary.en: Moab's fortress capital, the last hold-out in the allied campaign of Israel, Judah, and Edom against Mesha's rebellion — the siege broken off after the king of Moab offered his heir on the wall (2 Kings 3:25-27). Mesha's own account of the war survives on the Mesha Stele.

modernLocation.en: Tel Megiddo, Israel, commanding the Aruna pass into the Jezreel valley

summary.en: The chariot city guarding the great trunk road — fortified by Solomon (1 Kings 9:15), and the field where Josiah, intercepting Pharaoh Necho II's march to the Euphrates in 609 BC, was mortally wounded (2 Kings 23:29). Its twenty-plus superimposed cities made 'Har Megiddo' — Armageddon — a byword for battle.

modernLocation.en: On the Euphrates at the Syria-Turkey border, near Jerablus

summary.en: The Euphrates fortress where Nebuchadnezzar crushed the Egyptian and Assyrian remnant in 605 BC — 'concerning the army of Pharaoh-necho... which was by the river Euphrates in Carchemish' (Jeremiah 46:2) — opening the Levant to Babylon and setting Judah's final act in motion.

modernLocation.en: Tel Dan nature reserve at the foot of Mount Hermon, Israel

summary.en: Northernmost city of the land — 'from Dan even to Beersheba'. The Danites took Laish by the sword (Judges 18); Jeroboam I set one of the two golden calves here; and the Tel Dan Stele, found in its gate complex, carries an Aramean king's boast over the 'house of David'.

modernLocation.en: Tel Lachish, Shephelah of Judah, Israel

summary.en: Judah's second city. Joshua took it in the southern campaign (Joshua 10:31-32); Sennacherib besieged and stormed it in 701 BC — carving the assault in stone for his palace at Nineveh, while his siege ramp still lies against the tell; and its gate-room yielded the Lachish letters, written as Nebuchadnezzar's army closed in c. 588 BC (Jeremiah 34:7).
